news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh's mid-term treasury report lists 12 LOBO loans worth £122.4m outstanding at 30 September
news_drafts.lead:
City of Edinburgh Council had 12 LOBO loans totalling £122.4m outstanding at 30 September 2026, according to its Treasury Mid-Term Report 2026-2027, which goes to the Finance and Resources Committee. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it.

The debt table in Appendix 4 gives the coupons on the 12 loans as ranging from 4.375% to 5.25%. Their maturities run from 2028 to 2066.

The paper does not describe any lender call, repayment or replacement of the loans. The table shows them as outstanding at the date of the report.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh's plan shows a £14.3m gap for 2027/28, rising to £93.0m cumulatively by 2030/31
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council's medium-term financial plan forecasts a budget shortfall of £14.3m in 2027/28. The cumulative funding gap, excluding the Edinburgh Integration Joint Board (EIJB), which runs health and social care, rises to £47.3m in 2028/29, £70.8m in 2029/30 and £93.0m by 2030/31. The council's update to the plan, set out in February 2026, is in the papers for its meeting on 29 October.

A budget strategy progress update restates the 2027/28 gap from the June 2026 update. It says projections for later years are unchanged pending the Scottish Budget. The gap includes additional sums set aside for contract and other non-pay inflation, and the paper says there remains a risk around the adequacy of that provision. The council's external auditor says the council has developed medium and longer-term financial plans and that the plan shows it is financially sustainable in the short term. Its Exhibit 7 states: "There remain significant risks around long-term borrowing and funding gaps".

The council's share of the EIJB's projected gaps is shown separately: £19.7m in 2027/28, rising to £91.4m in 2030/31. Combined with the council's own gap, the total reaches £184.4m in 2030/31. The council's baseline planning assumption is that "the EIJB will address its own budget gaps without additional" council funding. It does not consider the EIJB's future pressures when developing savings plans, but says it will monitor any risk of overspend that could require additional council funding.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh: £4m empty-home premium for housing would raise 2027/28 funding gap from £14.3m to £18.3m
news_drafts.lead:
Dedicating £4m of new council tax income from second and long-term empty homes to housing projects would raise the City of Edinburgh Council's funding gap for 2027/28 from £14.3m to £18.3m. That is according to a report to its Policy and Sustainability Committee, which met on 20 October 2026. The gap is the further savings the council has still to find for that year, which the report calls its "incremental funding gap".

The money comes from the premium, an extra charge added to council tax on those homes. The report says the council had already assumed the new premium income when it set its 2026/27 budget, and estimates it at £4m in 2027/28. Dedicating it to new housing spending means it is not available to close the gap, which widens by the full £4m.

The report's wording is that "introducing new commitments in the way suggested in the motion would add up to £4m to the Council's incremental funding gap in 2027/28". The paper is headed "Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income".

findings.paper_title: 9.4 - IJB Audit and Assurance Committee - Draft Minute - 10.09.26
findings.headline: Nineteen EIJB internal audit actions remain open at 28 July 2026, none of them overdue
findings.detail: The committee was told that 19 internal audit actions were open, and none had passed their due date. The follow-up covered audits up to 28 July 2026. The Chief Internal Auditor was asked to report further on the Cyber Resilience Assurance Audit at a future meeting.
findings.matters: Open-action counts and whether any are overdue are a standard measure of remediation discipline that other councils and their partners can benchmark against.
findings.figures: 19 open actions; 0 overdue; progress up to 28 July 2026
findings.quote: It was highlighted that nineteen actions remained open, none of which were overdue.

findings.paper_title: 9.4 - IJB Audit and Assurance Committee - Draft Minute - 10.09.26
findings.headline: EIJB internal audit places 'Moderate Assurance' on its governance, risk management and internal controls for 2025/26
findings.detail: Internal Audit gave its overall conclusion on the adequacy of the EIJB's governance, risk management and internal control arrangements. The conclusion was supported by audit work through the year, progress on management actions, and assurance from partner organisations.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, can compare this rating with the internal audit opinion on their own integration joint board or partnership arrangements.
findings.quote: Internal Audit concluded that ‘Moderate Assurance’ could be placed on the adequacy of these elements

findings.headline: Prescribing is the main pressure in primary care, with a projected year-end overspend of £2.2m driven by weight management, ADHD and Freestyle Libre
findings.detail: The paper identifies growth in weight management drugs, ADHD medications and Freestyle Libre as the key drivers, with locum cover for maternity leave and sickness also adding cost in general medical services.
findings.matters: Growth in specific high-cost prescribing lines is a demand pressure that other councils and health partners see in their own budgets, and it is a line where forecasts can move quickly.
findings.figures: £2.2m prescribing overspend; primary care £4.3m overspend (2%); primary care budget £259,036k; forecast £263,377k
findings.quote: Prescribing remains the main financial pressure with a year-end overspend of £2.2m.

findings.headline: The March 2026 medium-term financial strategy identified a £26m savings requirement for 2026/27, with a £18m savings programme leaving a £8m residual imbalance in hosted and set-aside services
findings.detail: The paper says the residual imbalance relates entirely to hosted and set-aside services, which NHS Lothian has reiterated its commitment to address.
findings.matters: A residual gap that sits with a partner organisation rather than the integration authority itself is a structural arrangement other councils with similar shared services would want to understand.
findings.figures: £26m savings requirement for 2026/27; £92m requirement by 2028/29; £18m savings programme; £8m residual imbalance
findings.quote: a savings programme was agreed to deliver £18m, leaving a residual imbalance of £8m.

findings.headline: The Chief Finance Officer gives moderate assurance of a break-even position by 31 March 2027, conditional on NHS Lothian's commitment to working with the four Lothian integration authorities
findings.detail: The paper says the assurance rests on NHS Lothian's commitment to balance the hosted and set-aside budgets, and that risks will be monitored and escalated to the board.
findings.matters: A break-even forecast that depends on a partner's commitment, rather than on council-controlled actions, is a conditional position that other finance officers and lenders would want to track.
findings.figures: Moderate assurance; 31 March 2027 break-even date; 4 Lothian integration authorities
findings.quote: On the basis that NHS Lothian has committed to working with the 4 Lothian integration authorities to balance the hosted and set aside budgets, the Chief Finance Officer has provided moderate assurance that financial balance can be achieved by 31st March 2027.

daily_post.headline: Umega's management contract was extended to June 2030, and an insourcing review concluded that in-house provision was not viable at the current time.
daily_post.lead: A managing-agent contract running to 2030 fixes a major operating cost and dependency for the portfolio, and the insourcing review shows the council considered and rejected the alternative.
